title: Learning-rate schedules and indexing
description: Substitute every schedule index, apply changing rates to gradient descent, trace a plateau rule, and solve fresh practice.
source_short: Lecture4 PDF p.57 / exact reciprocal schedules / N4.4
source: Lecture4 PDF page57: reciprocal-linear, reciprocal-quadratic, exponential and stagnation-triggered multiplicative decay. numerical-practice.md N4.4; precise plateau counter is a labeled study extension.

pages.title: Read the exact schedule and its index
pages.subtitle: Lecture4 PDF page57 supplies these three formulas.
blocks: Eta-zero is the starting learning rate. k is the update index, beginning at zero. The rate at index k moves the current parameter to the next one.
The slide calls the first schedule linear decay and the second quadratic decay. Their denominators are linear and quadratic in k+1: both are reciprocal schedules.
In particular, linear here does not mean subtract a fixed amount from the rate. Beta is a positive exponential decay constant, separate from any momentum coefficient.

pages.title: Reciprocal linear: substitute k before dividing
pages.subtitle: Every denominator uses k+1, including the first update.
blocks: The drops are 0.06, 0.02 and 0.01, so the rate does not decrease by a constant amount. Starting at k=1 would incorrectly skip the original rate.

pages.title: Reciprocal quadratic: square the whole denominator
pages.subtitle: Parentheses determine which quantity is squared.
blocks: At k=2 the denominator is 9, not k-squared plus 1 = 5. It decays faster than the reciprocal-linear schedule with the same initial rate.

pages.title: Exponential: use the logarithm identity
pages.subtitle: Beta=ln2 means multiplying by one half at each update.
blocks: The natural logarithm ln2 is the number whose exponential is 2. A negative exponent makes the multiplier smaller as k increases.

pages.title: Compare the first four scheduled rates
pages.subtitle: All three agree at initialization, then decay differently.
blocks: These are alternative schedules. Do not apply all three successively to one rate unless a different rule explicitly says to combine them.
A rate table is not a parameter table: actual parameter changes also depend on the current gradient.

pages.title: See the rates over more update indices
pages.subtitle: The plotted points include k=0 rather than starting at k=1.
blocks: Exponential decay has a constant multiplicative ratio. The reciprocal schedules have ratios that vary with the update index. A lower rate does not automatically imply better training.

pages.title: Apply the rate with the matching current gradient
pages.subtitle: Use only reciprocal-linear decay in this worked parameter trace.
blocks: Notice both the rate and the gradient change. At update k=2, use the gradient at w2, then obtain w3. The first rate is not reused for every step.

pages.title: A plateau rule responds to measured progress
pages.subtitle: The lecture says reduce the rate when training or held-out performance stagnates.
blocks: For this study example, measure validation loss after each epoch. An epoch means a pass through the training examples; its count here begins at 1, unlike the update index k.
Chosen rule: improve only if the new validation loss is strictly below the best seen so far. After two consecutive epochs without improvement, multiply the current rate by 0.1.
Reset the no-improvement counter after a new best or a rate drop. The reduced rate takes effect in the next epoch. Retain the learned parameters.
This precise patience rule is an illustrative choice. Page57 gives the stagnation-triggered idea and multiplicative reduction, not these exact counter settings.

pages.title: Trace the plateau decision at every epoch
pages.subtitle: Best is the lowest validation loss observed; smaller is better.
blocks: Epoch 4 used rate 0.12; its decision sets rate 0.012 for epoch 5. The decision after epoch 7 sets rate 0.0012 for epoch 8. No earlier update is changed retroactively.

pages.title: Your turn: new initial rate and decay constant
pages.subtitle: Calculate the scheduled rate before updating a supplied parameter state.
blocks: Calculate reciprocal-linear, reciprocal-quadratic and exponential rates at k=2. Show the substituted denominator or exponent.
Using only the reciprocal-quadratic rate, calculate w3. This w2 is an independent supplied practice state, not the result of the earlier main-example updates.
Explain the difference between an update-index schedule and the epoch-based plateau rule.

pages.title: Practice: rates and the next parameter
pages.subtitle: Use k+1=3 before squaring the denominator.
blocks: The formula schedules change with k regardless of measured validation progress. The plateau rule changes only after its stated no-improvement trigger; it keeps the current learned parameters.
